data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Trace water through a landscape. Explain its changes and show why two drops may take different routes.

1. Read **Journey of a Raindrop**. Use Read Aloud or another reading support if helpful.
2. Open the **Glossary** and practice with the **Crossword** and **Word Scramble**.
3. Use **The Four Moves of Water** chart as a model. Its headings group ideas; they do not give every drop a fixed order.
4. Try **Sort It: Where Is the Water Going?**. Choose the process or storage shown by each card and explain your choice.
5. Complete **Check Your Understanding**. Use mistakes to decide what to review.
6. Use the **Sentence Frames** to explain two water pathways.
7. Open **Remember the Water Cycle**. Create a cue and explain one limit of your model.
8. Finish **Design Challenge: Where Should Our Rain Go?**. Make a proposal for the fictional schoolyard. Separate evidence from assumptions.

You may write, speak, draw, or use your communication device to explain your thinking.

I made a memory cue and explained its limits
I supported my schoolyard proposal with evidence

history.title: Journey of a Raindrop
history.data:
## Journey of a Raindrop

A puddle gets smaller on a sunny day. Where did the water go? Some liquid water changes into an invisible gas called **water vapor**. This change is **evaporation**. Energy is needed for it. Sunlight supplies much of that energy in Earth's water cycle, but water can evaporate at night too.

Plants take up water through their roots. Water vapor leaves through tiny pores in their leaves. This is **transpiration**. The amount depends on the plant and its surroundings.

As moist air cools enough, some vapor can change into liquid droplets. This is **condensation**. Tiny particles in the air help droplets form. Condensation also happens on cold surfaces near the ground, such as the outside of a cold glass.

Clouds contain tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both. Water vapor itself is invisible. Drops and ice particles can grow inside clouds. When particles fall through the air and reach the ground, we call this **precipitation**. Rain, snow, sleet, and hail are examples. Their form depends on conditions in the cloud and the air below it.

After rain, some water flows over the land as **runoff**. It may enter streams, lakes, or drains. Some water enters soil through infiltration. Part can stay as soil moisture and be used by plants or evaporate. Another part can move deeper and recharge **groundwater**.

Groundwater is water in the saturated zone below the water table. There, water fills the pores and cracks in soil or rock. Soil above that zone can hold both air and water. Water soaking into soil does not all become groundwater at once. Groundwater can move and flow into streams; it is not a still underground lake everywhere.

In this lesson, **collection** means water gathering or being stored. Oceans, lakes, rivers, soil, groundwater, and ice hold water for different lengths of time. **Gravity** helps water fall and flow downhill. Solar energy helps drive evaporation. Wind also moves water through the atmosphere.

The water **cycle** connects many routes. It has no single starting point or fixed order for every drop. Rain can return to the air from a puddle without going through a river. Water in ice may stay there much longer. We can trace possible journeys, but this lesson cannot tell the exact age or past route of the water in a bottle.

data.def: The change of liquid water into water vapor. It needs energy and can happen without direct sunlight.
The change of water vapor into liquid droplets, in air or on a surface.
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
Here, water gathering or being stored in places such as lakes, ice, soil, and the ground.
Water leaving a plant through tiny holes in its leaves and entering the air as vapor.
Water that flows over the land surface into streams and rivers instead of soaking in.
Water below the water table, where the pores and cracks in soil or rock are filled with water.
Water in its gas form — invisible and mixed into the air.
The force that pulls precipitation down to Earth and pulls rivers toward the ocean.
A repeating system of changes. Water can follow different routes within its cycle.

data.title: Remember the Water Cycle
data.instructions: Each card locks in one set of facts from Journey of a Raindrop. Study the example aid, then build or personalize your own and explain how it points back to the real science.

cards.target: Four useful water-cycle terms, with more than one possible route
essentialFacts: Evaporation changes liquid water into vapor and needs energy.
Condensation changes water vapor into liquid droplets.
Precipitation is water falling from clouds and reaching the ground.
Collection groups examples of gathering and storage; not every drop follows a fixed sequence.
cards.aiExample: Every Cloud Pours Carefully. E-C-P-C: Evaporation, Condensation, Precipitation, Collection.
cards.mapping: E-C-P-C recalls four terms in a simple model. It is not a rule for the route of every drop. A puddle can evaporate without first joining a river.
scaffoldSteps: Write E, C, P, C and name each term.
Choose a cue word for each letter.
Describe a different possible pathway and explain the limit of your cue.
coachPrompts: Which letter is repeated, and how will your sentence keep the two C words from swapping places?
Does your sentence hint at what each move does, or only at its letter?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own four-word sentence for E-C-P-C, or change the example so it sounds like you.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Explain how each word in your sentence leads back to one move of the water cycle.

hookFact.text: The water cycle connects many pathways and has no single starting point.

cards.target: Water vapor is invisible; the white mist you can see is already liquid droplets
essentialFacts: The visible mist in the kettle illustration is made of tiny liquid droplets. Clouds may contain liquid droplets, ice crystals, or both.
Cooling can change some vapor into droplets. The picture illustrates a process; it cannot show every invisible molecule.
cards.aiExample: Picture a kettle. The empty-looking gap just above the spout is the invisible vapor. The white plume only begins where the air is cool enough for droplets to form. Clear gap = gas. White cloud = liquid.
cards.mapping: The picture puts the two ideas side by side in one place you have seen: the gap stands for vapor you cannot see, and the plume stands for droplets you can.
cards.scaffoldStarter: When I picture ____, the invisible part is ____ and the white part is ____.
scaffoldSteps: Choose an illustration of a kettle, cold breath, or shower mist.
Distinguish the invisible gas from visible droplets.
Explain why visible ice crystals are also water, so visible water is not always liquid.
coachPrompts: Where exactly in your picture is the vapor, and how do you know it is there if you cannot see it?
What cooled the vapor enough to make droplets in your scene?
cards.studentPrompt: Describe or sketch your own scene that separates invisible vapor from visible droplets.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture help you remember that vapor is invisible?

hookFact.text: Water vapor is invisible; clouds can contain liquid droplets, ice crystals, or both.

cards.target: Distinguish runoff, infiltration, soil moisture, and groundwater
essentialFacts: Runoff moves over the land surface. Infiltration is water entering soil.
Some infiltrated water stays as soil moisture; some is used by plants or evaporates.
Some water moves deeper and recharges groundwater below the water table.
cards.aiExample: Three drops land on a hill. One runs along the surface into a stream. One enters soil and is later taken up by a plant. One moves deeper into the saturated zone. These are possible routes, not predictions for every hill.
cards.mapping: The first drop shows runoff. Both other drops infiltrate. Only the drop reaching the saturated zone joins groundwater; entering soil alone does not tell us that.
cards.scaffoldStarter: One drop runs over ____. A second enters soil and ____. A third reaches ____ below the water table.
scaffoldSteps: Trace a surface route and two possible routes through soil.
Mark which route reaches groundwater and what remains uncertain.
coachPrompts: What evidence would show water stayed in soil rather than reaching the water table?
How could soil conditions change the balance of runoff and infiltration?
cards.studentPrompt: Draw, describe, or act out three possible drop journeys.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Explain why infiltration and groundwater are different ideas.

hookFact.text: Soil above the water table can contain both air and water; the saturated zone has water-filled pores and cracks.

history.title: Sort It: Where Is the Water Going?

items.content: A puddle shrinks on a sunny sidewalk
A tree releases water through its leaves
Your cold drink glass gets wet on the outside
Tiny floating droplets crowd together in the sky
Hail bounces off a car roof
Water fills pores and cracks below the water table
A river carries water toward the ocean
Hot soup sends invisible water vapor into the air
Fog forms over a cold field in the morning

questions.question: A shallow dish holds water on a sunny day. No water leaks or spills, but its level falls. What happened?
options: It soaked down into the concrete and stayed there as liquid
The Sun's heat destroyed the water completely
It broke apart into oxygen and hydrogen gas
It changed into water vapor and mixed into the air
questions.correctAnswer: It changed into water vapor and mixed into the air

questions.question: What is a cloud made of?
options: Tiny floating water droplets and ice crystals
Smoke collected from the ground
Water vapor only, with no liquid or ice at all
Cotton-like fibers of frozen air
questions.correctAnswer: Tiny floating water droplets and ice crystals

questions.question: Why can droplets form on the outside of a cold glass?
options: The glass pushes dry air into tiny drops
Water vapor cools at the surface and becomes liquid
Gravity disappears near cold objects
Water is made from the solid glass
questions.correctAnswer: Water vapor cools at the surface and becomes liquid

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a form of precipitation?
options: Snow falling on a mountain
Hail bouncing off a roof
Fog sitting over a field
Sleet hitting a window

questions.question: Rain lands in a puddle and later evaporates. What does this show?
options: Water can return to the air without first reaching a river
Every drop must visit the ocean before it can evaporate
Water in a puddle cannot be part of the water cycle
Every drop follows the same route in the same amount of time
questions.correctAnswer: Water can return to the air without first reaching a river

questions.question: Rain enters soil. Does all of it immediately become groundwater? Explain how runoff, soil moisture, and groundwater differ.
questions.expectedAnswer: No. Runoff flows over the land. Infiltrated water may stay as soil moisture, be used by plants, or evaporate. Some moves deeper to recharge groundwater below the water table, where pores and cracks are filled with water.

questions.question: How do solar energy and gravity help drive the water cycle?
questions.expectedAnswer: Solar energy helps drive evaporation. Gravity pulls precipitation down and helps water flow downhill. Water vapor mixes with air; the Sun does not directly pull water upward.

history.title: But Wait — Water Questions Kids Actually Ask

data.question: Can we know exactly where the water in my bottle has been?
data.answer: Not from this lesson. Earth has cycled water for a very long time, but a bottle contains a mixture. We can suggest possible pathways without claiming a known age or a visit to a particular dinosaur.

data.question: Why doesn't the ocean overflow if rivers keep pouring into it?
data.answer: Evaporation removes water from the ocean; rain and flow from land add water. These flows are large and vary over time. They need not balance exactly in each year, and ocean level can change.

data.question: Why is rain fresh water when it evaporates from the salty ocean? 🧂
data.answer: Dissolved salt stays behind when water evaporates. Rain can pick up particles and dissolved substances from the air. Low salt does not mean rainwater is safe to drink.

data.question: Does every drop follow the four chart headings in order?
data.answer: No. The chart is a simple model. A puddle can evaporate before its water reaches a stream. Water may remain in ice, soil, or groundwater for very different lengths of time.

data.question: Where does my breath fog go on a cold day?
data.answer: That IS the water cycle, in miniature! Warm water vapor from your lungs hits cold air and condenses into tiny droplets — a little personal cloud — then evaporates again into the air.

data.question: Is snow just frozen rain?
data.answer: Not exactly. Snow forms when water vapor turns straight into ice crystals inside a very cold cloud. Sleet is closer to frozen rain — raindrops that freeze on the way down.

history.title: Design Challenge: Where Should Our Rain Go?
history.meta: 6th Grade • Design brief • proposal with labeled sketch

data.title: Where Should Our Rain Go?
data.instructions: Use the fictional schoolyard brief to propose a rainwater plan. Compare options, label your sketch, and distinguish observations from assumptions. This is a classroom proposal, not a construction task.
data.fitReason: A design proposal uses evidence about runoff, infiltration, and storage while keeping groundwater recharge distinct from water entering soil.

brief.context: Fictional case: after heavy rain, water pools on a paved school play area and flows toward a street drain. Nearby garden beds later become dry. The principal asks a student team to compare possible changes before any real design work.
brief.audience: The principal and the facilities manager
brief.drivingQuestion: How should our school handle the rain that lands on the paved area so that more of it soaks in or gets stored instead of running straight into the street?
brief.seedDirection: Start from the two routes in the lesson: where on the grounds could runoff be slowed down, and where could water be given a chance to infiltrate?
lockedLessonFacts: Runoff moves over land; infiltration is water entering soil.
Some infiltrated water remains as soil moisture and may be used by plants or evaporate.
Some water can move deeper to recharge groundwater in the saturated zone below the water table.
Slope, soil, land cover, and how wet the ground already is affect water pathways.
A sketch of water entering soil does not prove that the water reaches an aquifer.
openQuestions: How much of the paved area drains toward the street, and how much toward the beds?
What kind of soil is under the grass and beds, and how fast does it soak up water?
Are there rules about what can be built on school grounds or connected to the storm drain?
How much rain falls in a typical storm here?
stakeholders: Students who use the play area
Facilities staff who maintain the lot
Neighbors downhill from the street drain
criteria: Less water leaves the grounds as runoff after a typical storm
The play area still drains and is safe to use
The plan uses at least four glossary words correctly
Every claim about where water will go is tied to a lesson fact or marked as an assumption
constraints: Make a paper or digital proposal; do not dig, alter drains, or build anything.
Use supplied observations or a teacher-approved classroom model.
Keep water away from building foundations in the proposal.
Mark assumptions and identify what qualified facilities staff would need to check.
brief.deliverable: A one-page proposal with a labeled sketch of the grounds showing where rain lands, where you want it to go, and one change that slows runoff or lets water soak in, plus a short explanation of the water-cycle reasoning behind it.

parallelExample.context: Fictional example: a class compares a smooth tray with a soil-filled tray using the same amount of water.
parallelExample.move: They record water leaving each tray and water retained in the soil. They discuss spill and measurement error. Water held in a shallow tray is evidence about storage, not proof of groundwater recharge.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Comparing the same input helps test runoff and storage claims. Naming what the model cannot show keeps the conclusion bounded.

supports.frameStarter: Right now rain that lands on ____ runs toward ____ because ____. We want more of it to ____.
frameChoices: Slow the runoff so it has time to soak in
Redirect the runoff toward soil or beds that need water
Store the water in a tank or pond for later use
Replace part of the pavement with a surface water can pass through
coachPrompts: Which of your claims about where the water goes could you check by watching the grounds during the next rain?
What happens to your design in a very heavy storm, or after a week of dry weather?
Which glossary word describes each arrow on your sketch?

data.coachHint: Trace surface flow, then distinguish water retained in soil from water that might recharge groundwater.
